title: Why You Shouldn’t Send Students Out Of Class For Time-Out ss-for-time-out/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues against the popular practice of sending misbehaving students to a neighboring classroom for time-out, despite its apparent appeal and sense of finality. He identifies three specific problems: students miss instructional time and often feel they've 'gotten away with something' rather than being caught up; the consequence is weaker because students can't see what they're missing, making it feel more like a break than a real deterrent; and teachers lose the ability to monitor whether a student shows genuine remorse before rejoining the class, since that judgment requires the student's presence. His alternative is keeping time-out inside the classroom, where students can still see and feel excluded from an environment they enjoy, and where a teacher can wait for a student to signal readiness and reflection before releasing them. He reframes time-out's purpose entirely: not a punishment for wrongdoing, but a structured opportunity for reflection and personal growth.
points: Sending students out of the classroom for time-out causes them to miss instruction and often feel they escaped consequences.
In-class time-out is a stronger deterrent because students can see and feel what they are missing.
Monitoring genuine remorse before releasing a student from time-out requires keeping them present in the room.
Time-out should be framed as an opportunity for personal reflection and growth, not simply a punishment.
For time-out to work, students must value being part of the classroom enough to find separation from it undesirable.
quotes: The biggest problem with out-of-class time-out is that your students will miss instruction time. Even if you send them with busywork or a reflection form , many will feel as if they got away with something.

For time-out to be effective, your students must feel like they’re missing something. When you send them out of your classroom this feeling is minimized because they’re unable to see what they’re no longer part of.
Another key to effective time-out is to wait until the student shows remorse before allowing them to return to their seat, which can only be done if they’re in the room with you.

Their willingness to follow this procedure , which must be taught and modeled in detail before putting into practice, is a reliable sign that they’ve reflected on their mistake and taken responsibility for it.
It must be a place that causes students to accept responsibility and vow not to make the same mistakes again.
Time-out, then, becomes not a break from the classroom or a shameful punishment, but an avenue through which your students can grow and mature and become better people.
